title: Contrast and Accessibility in Slide Design (blog explainer)

brief.story: A clear explainer of the post.

slides.title: Accessible Slides Are Better Slides
slides.notes: Every audience sees, hears and processes information differently. Here are simple fixes that make your slides work for every viewer, and clearer for everyone.

slides.title: Contrast Is the Foundation
bullets: 3:1 for large text and key graphics
slides.notes: Low contrast is the most common problem, and one of the easiest to fix. Aim for four and a half to one for normal text, and test with a checker.

slides.title: Never Rely on Colour Alone
bullets: Before: status shown in red or green text
After: "On track" and "Late" labels plus icons
slides.notes: Some viewers can't tell red from green. Give each status a label and an icon, and let colour be an extra cue, not the only one.

slides.title: Make Text Easy to Read
slides.notes: Big, plain, left-aligned text reads well in a room and on a small screen. Avoid script or very light fonts, and leave plenty of space.

slides.title: Video Needs Captions and Described Visuals
slides.notes: When a deck becomes a video, turn on captions and let the voice explain what a chart shows, not just say "as you can see here".

slides.title: Accessible Slides Make Better Videos
slides.notes: Accessible slides make better videos. On Pro, a.i. directs the video, designing each scene and timing animation to your narration. Try Basic first at powerpoint2vid.com.
